newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ not running to potential - Telecom's Shirtcliffe.
newsitem.headline: NZ not running to potential - Telecom's Shirtcliffe.

text.p: The chairman of New Zealand's largest listed company, Telecom Corp of New Zealand, said on Wednesday the New Zealand economy was not running to potential.
Peter Shirtcliffe made the comment after the company reported normalised annual earnings of NZ$770.5 million, a growth rate of 3.2 percent against 19.5 percent in the previous year.
"We are operating in a very flat, relatively low growth economy. I think we can do a lot better," Shirtcliffe said.

"It is our view that the New Zealand economy is not running to its potential and there do not appear to be plans... that will lead the economy to run to its potential," he told a briefing of analysts and journalists.
"The revelance of that to a company like Telecom is simply this: that we are highly leveraged into the performance of the domestic economy.

"To the extent that those that determine the external economic environment can do much better, and I believe they can, we ought to be able to look foward to sustainable growth rates in the five and six percent area if we get our act together
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand estimates New Zealand's sustainable growth rate at about 2.75 percent.
Shirtcliffe said competitiveness was needed right through every sector of the economy. Companies and the government should follow Telecom's lead and introduce contestability within.
This did not necessarily mean putting privatisation back on the political agenda, he added. Structural reform and commitment to maximising competitiveness, productivity and innovation were the keys.
"Linked with the correct emphasis on the monetary dimension will give a recreation of five or six percent growth in a practical way."
He said New Zealand had up until the 1990s had low growth averaging around 0.9 percent, but had been through a high growth spurt in the 1990s which benefited everybody.
"It is no coincidence in my view that that (high growth) followed a period of structural reform and reduced size of government, and a focus on competitiveness and innovation and productivity.
"We have lost a bit of enthusiasm for some of those things."
"If we can get to an environment where that becomes the focus again, a company like Telecom will get startling benefits from it."
